The answer is false. The hyperchromic effect predicts that the concentration of dsDNA must be greater.  The hyperchromic effect is the increase in UV absorbance of DNA when it is denatured from dsDNA to ssDNA. This is because the bases in the double helix are stacked on top of each other, which restricts the rotation around the bonds between the base pairs. This stacking leads to electronic interactions between the bases, which result in a decrease in absorbance at 260nm. When the DNA is denatured, the two strands separate and the bases are no longer stacked on top of each other. This means that the electronic interactions between the bases are eliminated and each base can absorb light at its maximum potential. Therefore, the hyperchromic effect predicts that the absorbance of ssDNA will be greater than that of dsDNA. Since absorbance is proportional to concentration, it follows that more ssDNA will be produced than dsDNA in a reaction, and therefore the concentration of ssDNA will be lower than that of dsDNA.

The presence of the -OH bond at the 2’ carbon in RNA makes it less stable than DNA as it enables the nearby phosphate to form a cyclic compound when the proton is removed in alkali solutions. DNA is more stable than RNA because the hydrogen is not present at the 2’ carbon, meaning that the ring structure cannot form and therefore the phosphate cannot undergo hydrolysis.

The first half of the statement is true, as the strength of the promoter sequence is indeed dependent upon its resemblance of the consensus sequence. However, the second half of the statement is false, as the strength of the promoter sequence does not dictate the total length of the DNA segment that will be transcribed into RNA molecules. Instead, the length of the DNA segment that will be transcribed into RNA molecules is determined by the position of the transcription start site and the position of the terminator sequence.
